title: Decimals: Order of Operations & Rates
subtitle: Which operation first, and how much per one.
objectives: Apply the order of operations to decimal calculations
Round a decimal to a given place
Compare two options using unit rate
Solve multi-step problems using all four operations

cards.title: 2 + 3 × 4 has one right answer, and it is not 20
cards.text: Two people can do the same calculation and get different results. That is why the order is fixed by rule, not by taste.

cards.title: Brackets, then multiply and divide, then add and subtract
cards.text: Work left to right inside each level. Multiplying and dividing rank equally, and so do adding and subtracting.

cards.title: Look at the digit to the right, and nothing else
cards.text: Find the place you are rounding to. Look at the one digit after it. Five or more rounds up.
points: **3.847 to one decimal place** — look at the 4. Stays 3.8.
**3.867 to one decimal place** — look at the 6. Becomes 3.9.
**Only the next digit matters.** Ignore the rest.
**3.8499 to one place is 3.8.** The 99 is irrelevant.

cards.title: A lap time is rounded, and the rounding decides the podium
cards.text: Timing runs to thousandths, then gets shown to hundredths. Which way a time rounds has ended real races.
points: **That is why timing keeps more digits** than it shows.

question.explain: Look at the second decimal, which is 7. Seven is five or more, so the 4 rounds up to 5.

cards.title: Good spot to pause
cards.text: Order and rounding done. Part 2 is rates — how much for exactly one. Your place is saved.

cards.title: The only fair way to compare two different sizes
cards.text: A 900 g box for ₱225 or a 1.5 kg box for ₱360. You cannot compare those until you work out what one unit costs.

cards.title: Divide until you have one of something
cards.text: A unit rate is how much of one thing there is for exactly one of another. It is always a division.
points: **The bigger box is cheaper per kilogram.**

question.text: A 2.5 kg bag costs ₱200. What is the price per kilogram?
question.explain: 200 ÷ 2.5 = 80. Divide the price by the amount to get the price for one.

cards.title: Damage per second is a unit rate
cards.text: A weapon that hits for 90 every 3 seconds beats one that hits for 40 every 1 second. The raw number lies.
points: **40 ÷ 1 = 40 per second.** The smaller hit wins.
**Big numbers on the card** are not the comparison.
**Every stat screen** is doing this division for you.

cards.title: Nutrition labels are unit rates
cards.text: Every label gives the amount per 100 g so that two different products can be compared honestly.
points: **Per 100 g** is a unit rate somebody calculated for you.
**Per serving is not**, because servings differ.
**That is the entire trick** of reading a label.

cards.title: Fuel economy is a rate you already read
cards.text: Litres per hundred kilometres, or kilometres per litre. Both are unit rates and they point in opposite directions.

question.text: Which is better value: 1.5 L for ₱90, or 2.5 L for ₱140?
options: They cost the same per litre
You cannot tell without more information
question.explain: 90 ÷ 1.5 = 60 and 140 ÷ 2.5 = 56. The larger one is cheaper per litre.

cards.title: Write down what each step means
cards.text: When a problem uses three operations, the mistake is almost never the arithmetic. It is losing track of what a number represents.
points: **Check the unit at the end.** Pesos, kilograms, litres.

question.text: You buy 3 items at ₱24.50 each and pay with ₱100. What change?
question.explain: 3 × 24.50 = 73.50, then 100 − 73.50 = 26.50. Two steps, and the second is the one people skip.

terms.def: Brackets, then multiply and divide, then add and subtract.
Replacing a number with a nearby simpler one, to a stated place.
A digit position after the point. 3.14 has two.
A comparison of two quantities with different units, such as pesos per kilogram.
A rate for exactly one of something. Always found by dividing.

cards.title: The four that matter
points: **Unit rate = divide until you have one.**
**Label every step.** The unit is the check.

quiz.text: A 4 L can of engine oil costs ₱260. What is the price per litre?
quiz.explain: 260 ÷ 4 = 65. A unit rate is always a division.

quiz.text: A car travels 180 km on 12 litres. What is the fuel economy?
quiz.explain: 180 ÷ 12 = 15 km per litre. Distance divided by fuel gives distance for one litre.

quiz.text: Relief rice: 750 g for ₱150, or 1.2 kg for ₱216. Which is better value?
quiz.explain: 150 ÷ 0.75 = 200 per kg, and 216 ÷ 1.2 = 180 per kg. The larger one is cheaper.

quiz.text: The cheaper total price is always the better value.

teacher.summary: Week 6 Math continues the decimal work and adds the two things Weeks 3 to 5 left out: the order of operations, and rates. The order is presented as a convention that exists because two people doing the same calculation must get the same answer, which is a better reason than an acronym. Rounding is reduced to a single instruction — look at the one digit to the right and nothing else — because looking at the whole tail is the commonest error. The unit rate half is the practically useful part: comparing two prices for different sizes is a real skill, and the nutrition label card points out that per-100 g exists exactly so that comparison is possible while per-serving quietly prevents it.
discussion: Give him two supermarket prices for different pack sizes and ask which is better. He will need the unit rate and there is no way round it.
Ask why 3.8499 rounds to 3.8 at one decimal place. Only the next digit counts, and that surprises people.
Ask why the order of operations has to be a rule rather than a preference. Two people, one calculation, two answers is the answer.
Ask him to check a label for per-100 g against per-serving on something in the cupboard.
teacher.extension: Give him a receipt and ask for the unit price of every item, then rank them. Real packaging sizes are deliberately awkward, which is the point.
misconceptions: 'Work left to right through everything.' Multiplication and division come before addition and subtraction.
'Rounding means looking at all the digits after.' Only the single digit to the right of the place matters.
'The bigger pack is always better value.' Often, but not always. The unit rate is the only way to know.
'A rate and a unit rate are the same.' A unit rate is specifically for exactly one of something.
